I oppose the proposed rule and urge DHS to withdraw it for the following reasons:
I. NO STATUTORY AUTHORITY: THE CHARGE IS A TAX
DHS relies on its general power to set "conditions" of nonimmigrant admission, INA 214(a). In Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump (Feb. 20, 2026), the Supreme Court held that a power to regulate does not include a power to tax. The charge is a tax under National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974): DHS admits it cannot keep the money, which goes to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts (31 U.S.C. 3302). The amount is tied to no cost of service, and its stated purpose is to deter OPT use. When Congress wanted an anti-fraud fee in INA 214, it enacted one expressly: $500 for certain H-1B and L petitions, earmarked for fraud detection (8 U.S.C. 1184(c)(12), 1356(v)). It has enacted no OPT charge. Washington Alliance v. DHS, 50 F.4th 164 (D.C. Cir. 2022), upheld OPT as a condition of status, not a power to raise revenue. With $109.4 billion in ten-year transfers, West Virginia v. EPA requires clear authorization, and Loper Bright gives DHS's reading no deference. On June 8, 2026, the District of Massachusetts vacated the $100,000 H-1B charge as an unlawful tax, and the First Circuit denied a stay on July 24, 2026.
II. ARBITRARY AND CAPRICIOUS: THE FEE DOES NOT FIT THE FRAUD
State Farm requires a rational connection between the facts found and the choice made. DHS's largest figure, 10,000 students at "suspect" employers, is about 3% of 2024 participants (194,554 OPT plus STEM OPT), and DHS does not say how many cases were confirmed. Every case DHS cites involves employers or document vendors, and every one was found with existing tools: prosecutions, SEVIS data, site visits. Yet the fee is charged to schools, often before any employer exists, since students may apply up to 90 days before completion without a job offer. A change of employer triggers no new fee. A fee that never sees the employer cannot deter employer fraud. DHS also charges $30,000 on STEM OPT, the track that already requires I-983 training plans, E-Verify and site visits. DHS rejected extending those safeguards without estimating their cost, and never considered employer attestation, registration or debarment, or its existing power to withdraw SEVP certification.
III. FLAWED ANALYSIS AND IGNORED RELIANCE
DHS projects $12.8 billion a year by applying the fees to historic participation, while conceding that schools will decline to pay. If the fee deters, the revenue figure is wrong. If the revenue materializes, the fee has not deterred. DHS quantifies no effects on enrollment, tax revenue or research staffing. Its wage evidence relies on 2001 data, and it admits it cannot quantify OPT's labor impact. It concedes schools may pass the cost to "all students," meaning American students. DHS v. Regents requires weighing reliance interests. DHS calls them "far outweighed" without measuring any. Students now enrolled chose schools and took on debt in reliance on OPT carrying no school charge, and in the transition year even students moving into STEM OPT would face $70,000. 1,389 of 2,478 affected schools (56%) are small entities, yet DHS did not consider tiered fees, caps, phase-ins or exempting pre-completion OPT (5 U.S.C. 603(c)).
IV. BROKEN BENCHMARK AND INADEQUATE PROCESS
DHS set $70,000 to be "comparable" to an H-1B charge that a court has since held unlawful. A single summer internship would trigger $70,000, and $100,000 with later OPT. DHS gave only 30 days to comment on the rule itself but 60 days on paperwork burden. Executive Orders 12866 and 13563 call for at least 60 days.

After reading the proposed rule to add Optional Practical Training fees, I noticed some issues with the proposed rule that I would like to point out. Requiring schools to pay the fees, regardless of whether they can pass off the cost to the students or employers, adds an extra burden on schools in a time when institutions are already doing more with less when it comes to resources. Even schools with a small number of students applying for OPT would make payments of over $1 million each application cycle, which in not feasible. If the fees are passed off to students or employers, schools would have to create a payment process to make it possible, using time and resources that could be used on other processes that benefit the schools. 

With the proposed fees being deposited into the Treasury, how can schools be sure the money is going toward Optional Practical Training rather than other government priorities? If the government is concerned with fraud, I would suggest a discussion with people who are directly working with students participating in Optional Practical Training in schools and with employers. Charging more money to apply for Optional Practical Training authorization will not change any allegations of fraud. A conversation to figure out the methods of alleged fraud and how to prevent it would make more of difference than charging fees.

Many international students choose to study in the United States for the added benefit of Optional Practical Training. Other countries have taken notice and have started to add practical training to the options for international students, which has made the international education market more competitive. Adding the proposed fees will have more of a chilling effect and decrease the total number of international students studying in the United States moving forward. The students who are already here will be at a disadvantage since they came with the understanding that Optional Practical Training would be an option for them, but if the proposed fees are implemented, practical training may be out of reach due to financial constraints. When international students are admitted to universities, they must show financial proof of funding for one year of study. They can plan ahead for the rest of their program of study and the current application fees for Optional Practical Training charged by USCIS, but they could not foresee the additional fees proposed in this rule. The fact that these fees cost more than one year of study in many schools is also an additional financial burden that may keep students away and send them home at the end of their program of study. 

The decrease in the total number of international students and international students participating in Optional Practical Training does not only affect the students themselves. The loss of revenue impacts local communities and their economies. International students spend money on rent, utilities, food, vehicles, and other necessities when living in the United States in addition to their tuition costs. With less international students, the rental market in college towns is greatly impacted, which affects local landlords. 

Bringing international students to the United States is not only beneficial for them, but for domestic students as well. In an increasingly global world, American students need to be prepared to work in diverse environments. Upon graduation, American students can say they have worked with diverse groups of people in their classes, in university clubs, and athletics. In offering Optional Practical Training, international students can also learn about American work culture and take those ideas home with them when they return at the end of their practical training experience. 

With a decrease in international student numbers comes a decrease in the number of staff needed to monitor their immigration records, negatively impacting American workers in the field of international education. The field has already been hit with a wave of layoffs and firings as reactions to other government policies which have had a chilling effect on international student numbers. This proposed rule is yet another blow to the field and leaves international student advisors wondering if the field will continue to be a viable career path moving forward. 

In conclusion, the proposed rule to add exorbitant fees to Optional Practical Training will have multiple negative consequences, not only impacting international students, but American workers and the U.S. economy. The money collected from the fees is not guaranteed to be put toward improving the Optional Practical Training program and the idea of collecting these fees will have a chilling effect on the number of international students due to the uncertainty of planning to study in the United States. Please reconsider the proposed fees and find other solutions that do not add unnecessary burdens to schools and international students.

I'm an F-1 student, and I'm asking DHS to withdraw this rule.

Imagine if an American student went to study abroad, and partway through, that country's government announced she now owed $70,000 just to do the practical training every other student there was already doing — training directly tied to her degree, something she'd planned her academic and financial life around. Not because she'd done anything wrong, but because a small number of people had abused the system and the government decided it was easier to charge everyone than go after the people actually responsible. Most Americans would call that outrageous. That's exactly what this rule does to us.

I came here the way most international students do: left my family, left what was familiar, took on debt, and accepted a huge amount of uncertainty — a visa that can be revoked, a status that depends on staying enrolled, no guarantee any of it pays off. We don't get federal aid. We don't get the safety net American students have. We earn our admission, we earn our grades, and if we want practical training, we compete for it like everyone else, 10,000 miles from home with no backup plan. A $70,000 upfront fee isn't a "deterrent to fraud" — fraud is already illegal, and DHS's own numbers show the fraud it's worried about touches a small fraction of OPT participants. What this fee actually does is price out almost everyone, guilty or not.

The rule also claims to protect American workers from unfair competition. But if an American graduate is genuinely the stronger candidate, she doesn't need a $70,000 wall built around the job market to win it — she just gets hired, the same way qualified people already do on both sides. Competing against international students isn't what makes jobs scarce. If anything, we're the ones taking the harder road: no family nearby, no safety net, a status that can end with a single email, and we choose to work hard anyway. Nobody is "scared" of sponsorship costs — employers already factor that in when they decide whether to sponsor someone, and most students never get sponsored at all. What this rule does is make sure almost nobody even gets the chance to try.

I'm not asking for a free pass. I'm asking to be treated the way this country has always said it treats people: let merit decide, go after the people who actually commit fraud, and don't punish hundreds of thousands of students who did nothing but work hard and follow the rules. If Americans believe they're capable, let the competition stay fair and open, the same uncertainty and effort on both sides. DHS should withdraw this rule — or at minimum, scale it down to actually match the problem it claims to solve, instead of a fee that functions as a ban dressed up as policy.

I am writing to submit a public comment in strong opposition to the proposed rule establishing new fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT). As an international student currently studying in the United States on an F-1 visa, I am directly impacted by this proposed regulation.

I urge DHS to rescind the proposed fee structure of $70,000 for an initial OPT application and $30,000 for subsequent applications. The proposed fees are astronomically disproportionate to the actual cost of administering the OPT program and far exceed the financial capacity of the vast majority of international students. I believe it would be easier and more bearable if the proposed fee structure for an initial OPT application would be $30000 or less and even lesser amount for subsequent applications.

As an F-1 student, I am already required to pay substantial tuition, often at out-of-state or international rates, as well as significant SEVIS fees and application costs just to maintain my legal status. Adding a $70,000 fee to the OPT application process is not just a deterrent; it is an absolute barrier. If this rule is finalized, I, like many of my peers, would be entirely priced out of gaining practical experience in my field of study. Even the proposed $30,000 fee for subsequent applications is an impossible sum for a recent graduate. While the rule notes that the fee does not have to be paid by the school, assuming a student or an employer can easily absorb a $70,000 cost demonstrates a profound misunderstanding of the financial realities of early-career professionals. International students bring unique perspectives and specialized skills, particularly in STEM fields, which are vital to U.S. innovation and economic competitiveness. Pricing them out of the workforce will harm U.S. employers who rely on this talent pipeline.

Therefore, I strongly recommend that DHS withdraw this proposed rule entirely. I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. It relies on selective examples, unsupported assumptions, conflicting data, and a flawed cost-benefit analysis. As a current PhD student at a research university, I see firsthand how critical OPT is to advancing research and bringing incredible minds to work in this country. 

**1. Selective evidence (Sec. IV.A)**
DHS cites a 2020 conviction, 15 arrests that year, a 2021 news story, 2025 site visits, and an ICE YouTube video. The text says the video identified 10,000 students working for suspicious employers, while footnote 56 says 10,000 suspicious employers. Either way, suspicion is not proof, and 10,000 is only about 3% of the roughly 290,000 OPT and STEM OPT participants in 2024. Most cited cases involve employer fraud uncovered through existing site visits and prosecutions, yet DHS says the fee is "not tied to a specific employer." There is no evidence this fee would have prevented the foreign-agent case DHS cites.

**2. Conflicting data**
DHS claims STEM OPT has "far surpassed" the 2016 projection of roughly 92,000 participants by year 10 and is "nearly double" the H-1B cap, citing 165,524 participants. But its own analysis reports 95,384 STEM OPT authorizations in 2024, consistent with the projection and close to the 85,000 annual H-1B cap. Its labor-market claims, including a study using 2001 data on foreign computer workers, come from a Presidential Proclamation, not an analysis of OPT wages. STEM OPT already requires comparable wages (Form I-983).

**3. High fees do not prevent fraud (Sec. IV.C)**
DHS assumes schools will recommend only "the most promising students," but a high fee measures ability to pay, not merit or honesty. DHS acknowledges that schools may pass the cost to students or employers. Employers already selling job letters can build the fee into their prices, while honest students who cannot afford $70,000 are excluded. DHS provides no evidence that any fee level would reduce fraud.

**4. This is a tax, not a fee**
The money goes to the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, generating an estimated $8.7–16.9 billion annually. DHS's own PRA supporting statement says SEVP fees must cover program costs (8 U.S.C. 1356(m); 31 U.S.C. 9701). This fee recovers no costs; it is modeled on an H-1B fee to discourage participation. That makes it an unauthorized tax (National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974)). INA 214(a)'s authority over "time and conditions" cannot justify a $109 billion levy. The 2020 Ombudsman report DHS cites blames fraud on compliance resources failing to keep pace with the program, yet none of this money would fund compliance. DHS also suggests it may end OPT without the fees, while admitting it cannot keep the revenue.

**5. Flawed cost-benefit analysis (Sec. VII.A)**
DHS leaves benefits unquantified while estimating costs of up to $8.2 billion annually. It caps lost-OPT costs at the unpaid fee, arguing parties "could collectively cost share" if OPT were worth more. This is circular: much of OPT's value, including innovation, taxes, and local spending, benefits the public, not just whoever pays. DHS also fails to model enrollment losses, an omission the Presidents' Alliance court found likely unlawful under Michigan v. EPA, 576 U.S. 743 (2015).

**6. Alternatives dismissed**
DHS rejects site visits, training plans, and employer checks as too slow or costly, despite relying on those tools to uncover the fraud it cites. GAO-19-297, also cited by DHS, found OPT oversight had improved. Administrative convenience is not reasoned decision-making under State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983).

**7. Reliance and unintended consequences**
DHS calls reliance speculative because only about 20% of F-1 students use OPT. That still represents roughly 280,000 people who planned careers and took on debt based on the program. Pre- plus post-completion OPT costs $100,000, versus $70,000 for post-completion alone, penalizing students who combine work and study. Refund denials also cannot be appealed.

**8. Small institutions and states**
In the transition year, 841 small institutions (60.5%) face costs above 1% of revenue, and 116 face costs above 20%, yet DHS offers no relief. The UMRA section first says the rule falls below the threshold, then says it exceeds it. DHS consulted no state officials and claims no federalism impact, despite requiring 1,044 state institutions to pay.

**9. Process and baseline**
DHS allows 32 days to comment on a $109 billion rule but 60 days for a paperwork change estimated to take five minutes. It also relies on the Duration of Status rule (91 FR 44976) as its baseline and vetting rationale without noting that the rule has been postponed. The comment period should be extended to at least 60 days.

Why Protecting Optional Practical Training (OPT) Matters

Optional Practical Training (OPT) plays an important role in maintaining the United States' position as a leading destination for international talent. For community colleges, particularly those offering career and technical education programs, OPT helps strengthen relationships with local businesses, supports regional workforce needs, and makes their programs more attractive to international students. It also supports international student recruitment and institutional competitiveness by providing opportunities to connect classroom learning with professional experience. Restricting or eliminating OPT could weaken these opportunities and limit the contributions international students make to local economies and communities.

Protecting OPT is not simply about supporting international students. It is about strengthening the U.S. economy, supporting American employers, encouraging innovation, and preserving the country's global competitiveness. Maintaining OPT benefits students, educational institutions, employers, and the communities they serve.

The fee does not fund the problem it names. DHS says it cannot police OPT without these fees, then states the money goes to Treasury under 31 U.S.C. 3302 and that ICE has no authority to retain it. If the issue is that roughly 6,186 certified schools are covered by about 60 field representatives, collecting up to $144 billion over ten years and sending none of it to SEVP does not address that.

The fraud showing has no denominator. The preamble cites a 2020 conviction, a 2020 arrest of fifteen students, a 2021 news article, site visits in Northern Virginia, and an announced investigation. Against 194,554 OPT and 165,524 STEM OPT participants in 2024, DHS never states a non-compliance rate or a trend. “Rampant fraud” is a quantitative claim and the rule never quantifies it. Nor would any cited incident have been prevented by a school paying a fee before entering a SEVIS recommendation; the 2020 conviction involved a vendor selling forged employment letters, which a university payment does not detect.

The amounts are not derived from anything. DHS performs no cost-of-service or risk-based calculation. It states it chose a figure comparable to H-1B fees, equating twelve months of entry-level training with a multi-year professional classification the INA treats differently. The claim that the fees match one or two years of educational costs is inaccurate for most institutions and irrelevant to administrative cost.

The participation estimates contradict DHS’s own data. The high scenario assumes no change in participation. Weeks earlier, in the technical appendix to its proposed $103,265 H-1B rule, DHS reported a 91.2 percent decline in initial I-129 H-1B petitions after the $100,000 payment, which the September 18, 2026 proclamation indicates was paid for roughly 700 individuals. The rule never explains why universities would pay $70,000 for twelve months when employers would not pay $100,000 for multi-year hires. The low scenario is separately inconsistent: 88,374 initial fees alongside 74,088 STEM participants implies an 84 percent continuation rate, against DHS’s own 2021–2024 figure of 56 percent. It assumes the fee suppresses entry while raising continuation by thirty points. Averaging these two produces no defensible estimate. Clemens (IZA DP 18933, September 2026) estimates a $100,000 practical-training tax cuts OPT starts by a third or more in every incidence scenario and about four fifths under university or employer incidence, the incidence this rule contemplates. DHS engages no elasticity literature.

Costs are quantified; benefits are not. DHS estimates $35.1 billion in ten-year primary costs, up to $69.9 billion, and quantifies no benefits, contrary to E.O. 13563 and Circular A-4. The opportunity-cost table measures lost value as fees not paid, which counts uncollected revenue rather than lost labor from graduates of U.S. degree programs.

The labor-market premise is unsupported, including by DHS’s own citation. No study is cited finding OPT harms U.S. workers. Zavodny’s analysis of ICE data (2008–2016, NFAP) found no such evidence and found lower U.S. STEM unemployment where OPT participation was higher. Kwon, Lee and Monràs (CEPR DP 21224, February 2026) found the 2016 STEM extension raised native high-skilled employment and wages by roughly 1 percent and increased firm creation. DHS’s lone economic citation is Bound, Khanna and Morales (NBER WP 23153); the rule quotes two distributional figures and omits the paper’s central finding that high-skilled immigration raised overall native welfare, lowered IT prices, and raised IT output 1.9 to 2.5 percent. BLS put computer and mathematical occupation unemployment at 3.3 percent in September 2026, down from 3.9 percent.

Practical training is part of the education. The rule calls student reliance on OPT speculative while its own history traces the “directly related to the major area of study” requirement to 1991 and earlier. In laboratory, clinical, engineering and computing fields, supervised applied work is how a degree is completed. International students contribute $42.9 billion and support 355,736 jobs annually (NAFSA, 2024–2025), before OPT work is counted.

Alternatives and reliance are not seriously considered. DHS identifies one alternative, extending STEM OPT requirements to OPT generally, and rejects it because a fee is faster to implement. Administrative convenience is not reasoned decision-making. Enrollment, tuition and research-staffing effects go unquantified. DHS estimates 56 percent of regulated institutions are small entities and declines to exempt them; at $70,000 per student, those institutions will simply stop recommending OPT, ending the program for their students without saying so.

Thesis and Statement of Opposition

This comment registers vehement opposition to the proposed OPT fee rule. Rather than functioning as a legitimate administrative cost-recovery mechanism, this rule operates as an unconstitutional, punitive tax designed to enact a de facto ban on the F-1 OPT program. This proposal violates the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), exceeds DHS’s statutory authority, and threatens catastrophic harm to U.S. economic competitiveness and the higher education sector. The proposed rule must be withdrawn immediately.

Legal Violations and Exceedance of Statutory Authority

Under the Independent Offices Appropriations Act (IOAA), federal agency fees must be reasonably tied to the actual administrative cost of providing a service. The current Form I-765 processing fee reflects this administrative burden. Inflating this to a combined $100,000 fee for a STEM graduate is not a user fee; it is a punitive tax, and DHS lacks the Article I constitutional authority to levy taxes, making this rule fundamentally illegal. Furthermore, the APA prohibits agency rules that lack a rational basis. There is zero rational connection between the nominal administrative burden of a Designated School Official (DSO) updating SEVIS and a $70,000 initial fee, meaning the rule fails the standard of reasoned decision-making. Finally, Congress established the F-1 visa category to promote global educational exchange, of which practical training has been a legally recognized and integral component for decades. By weaponizing exorbitant fees to functionally terminate the OPT program, DHS is attempting to rewrite the Immigration and Nationality Act through executive overreach.

Severe Economic Harm and Deterioration of U.S. Competitiveness

Because the rule allows universities to pass these costs to students, U.S. higher education will become instantly unaffordable for international applicants, who currently contribute billions to local economies and effectively subsidize tuition for domestic students. Pricing them out will result in severe budget shortfalls, program cuts, and potential bankruptcies for smaller U.S. colleges. Moreover, American companies rely heavily on the OPT and STEM OPT pipelines to fill critical gaps in technology, medicine, engineering, and artificial intelligence. Imposing a six-figure premium on every STEM graduate will destroy this talent pipeline, severely handicapping American businesses on the global stage. This rule also has a disproportionate impact on small businesses; the Regulatory Flexibility Act requires agencies to assess and mitigate impacts on small entities, yet small U.S. businesses and tech startups that hire specialized OPT graduates cannot afford to absorb these exorbitant costs and will lose vital access to global talent, heavily favoring only the largest monopoly corporations.

Material Public Impact and Discourse Evidence

Real-time discourse on public forums like Reddit demonstrates that the public immediately recognizes this rule as an intimidation tactic aimed at forcing schools to abandon OPT recommendations. It is widely viewed not as a regulatory adjustment, but as a deliberate mechanism to kill the program without explicitly banning it. This commentary reveals that prospective and current international students are already making plans to transfer their academic pursuits and future entrepreneurial endeavors to competing nations like Canada, the UK, and Australia, taking their specialized skills and tax revenues out of the U.S. labor market permanently. Finally, while proponents of restricting OPT frequently argue that international students are hired strictly for payroll tax (FICA) exemptions, public discourse rightly criticizes this flawed logic; the proposed $70,000 baseline fee exponentially eclipses any minor payroll tax savings an employer might realize. This mathematical reality proves the fee is designed solely to act as an insurmountable barrier, not a tool to "level the playing field" for domestic workers.

I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees and urge DHS to withdraw the rule. It rests on selective anecdotes, untested assumptions, inconsistent data, and an incomplete cost-benefit analysis.

I strongly oppose the proposed rule, “Optional Practical Training Fees” (Docket ICEB-2026-0100). Its central mistake is treating the price of participation as evidence of compliance. A university’s ability to pay $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation, and $30,000 for a subsequent one, tells DHS little about whether a job is genuine, whether a student is qualified, or whether an employer is obeying the law.

First, the rule confuses deterrence with fraud detection. Fraudulent conduct involves identifiable acts: fabricated employment, false worksites, misleading records, and violations by employers or schools. Charging every institution a very large fee does not verify any of those facts. It simply reduces the number of people able to participate. DHS should explain why legitimate participants must bear a universal financial penalty instead of directing resources toward employers and institutions with concrete warning signs.

Second, the proposal risks rewarding wealth rather than merit. Two equally talented graduates could receive different outcomes solely because one attends a wealthy university and the other attends a regional public institution with a limited budget. The same problem arises for employers: a large corporation may be able to absorb or subsidize a charge that a small technology company, laboratory, or startup cannot. None of these distinctions measures educational value or immigration compliance. They measure access to money.

Third, the proposed rule would transfer costs to people who are not accused of wrongdoing. DHS acknowledges that schools might spread the charge among international students, domestic students, and employers. Faced with such costs, colleges may cut programs, reduce financial aid, or increase tuition. International enrollment could decline, further eroding tuition revenue that helps sustain campuses and the surrounding communities. American students, faculty, local businesses, and taxpayers would feel the consequences. A policy advertised as protecting Americans should not ignore these burdens on Americans.

Fourth, the rule could undermine the research and innovation ecosystem. American universities train engineers, scientists, and other specialists whose knowledge can be applied in laboratories, businesses, and public-sector projects. OPT offers a limited period to put that training into practice. Removing this opportunity through an unaffordable financial barrier may encourage students to study and build careers elsewhere from the outset. The United States pays a long-term price when ideas, future companies, and highly trained people move to competing economies. A policy aimed at preventing misuse must account for what the country gives up when lawful talent is driven away.

Fifth, the proposal's economic justification is unconvincing. DHS's own regulatory analysis assigns no estimate to annualized monetized benefits, while its primary estimate puts annualized costs at approximately $4.1 billion. It also recognizes the possibility of reduced international enrollment, lost graduate earnings, and lost employer productivity. Without a credible estimate of how much fraud the fee would prevent, it is impossible to conclude that the expected benefits justify such extraordinary costs. Nor does a reduction in OPT participation, by itself, demonstrate a corresponding reduction in fraud.

Sixth, the proposed payment does not directly finance the promised oversight. DHS explains that collected fees would enter the U.S. Treasury as miscellaneous receipts, rather than being retained by ICE or earmarked for OPT compliance investigations. That raises a basic question: how does collecting billions of dollars from universities strengthen enforcement if the funds are not dedicated to investigators, employer verification, or better monitoring systems? The proposal appears to rely mainly on exclusion rather than more effective detection.

The more rational approach is to improve the rules where abuse actually occurs. DHS could prioritize investigations of shell employers, validate actual worksites and payroll records, apply meaningful penalties to repeated violators, and expand targeted compliance checks. It should evaluate these alternatives against the proposed fee using measurable outcomes, including fraud identified, enforcement costs, effects on tuition and enrollment, and lost economic activity.

America's universities and research institutions are national assets. They should not be forced to choose between supporting legitimate graduates and protecting their own financial health. DHS should withdraw this proposal and pursue evidence-based enforcement that safeguards program integrity without sacrificing the nation's education system and economic future.

Reference: 91 FR 64566, October 8, 2026; Proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(2)

I am an international Master student in Architecture who has dedicated years to pursuing advanced education, conducting research, and gaining professional experience in the United States. I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee under 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(2).

1. Disproportionate Financial Burden on Universities and Students (Sections IV.C and VII.A.4)

In Section IV.C (91 FR 64575), DHS explicitly acknowledges that educational institutions may pass the financial burden of these fees onto international students, other students, or employers. This raises a serious concern: even though universities are officially responsible for paying the fees, students could ultimately bear the costs.

Furthermore, DHS estimates in Section VII.A.4 (91 FR 64583, Table 3) that the proposed fees could generate between $8.4 billion and $16.5 billion annually, with a primary estimate of $12.4 billion. These figures demonstrate the extraordinary financial scale of the proposal.

Many universities, particularly smaller institutions and publicly funded research universities, may be unable to absorb these costs. As a result, qualified students could lose access to practical training simply because their institutions cannot afford the fees.

2. Financial Ability Does Not Establish Academic Merit or Prevent Fraud (Sections IV.A and IV.C)

In Section IV.A (91 FR 64570–64571), DHS describes fraudulent employment arrangements, including shell companies and nonexistent workplaces. I recognize the seriousness of these concerns and support stronger enforcement against such activities.

However, Section IV.C (91 FR 64574) suggests that requiring substantial fees would encourage institutions to recommend only highly qualified students. Financial capacity is not an appropriate measure of academic achievement, professional qualifications, or compliance with immigration regulations.

A student who has maintained lawful status, successfully completed an advanced degree, and secured legitimate training should not be denied an opportunity solely because their university cannot pay $70,000.

DHS should instead prioritize targeted employer verification, compliance investigations, and enforcement against fraudulent entities rather than imposing financial barriers on all students.

3. Negative Consequences for Research and STEM Education (Sections VI and VII.A.5)

In Section VI (91 FR 64578), DHS recognizes that the proposed fees could affect institutions’ existing budgets and suggests that universities could mitigate those impacts by transferring the costs to students or employers.

This approach does not eliminate the financial burden; it simply transfers it to another party.

For international graduate students in engineering and other STEM fields, practical training provides an opportunity to apply years of specialized education and research to real-world challenges. These experiences can benefit American businesses, infrastructure development, and technological innovation.

The proposed fees could discourage universities from supporting OPT participation, limit access to professional training, and make the United States less attractive to talented international researchers.

4. Opposition to Repeated Fees at Higher Educational Levels (Section V.A)

In Section V.A (91 FR 64577), DHS specifically requests public comments on an alternative that would impose an additional $70,000 initial OPT fee whenever a student advances to a higher educational level.

I strongly oppose this alternative. Students who continue from bachelor’s to master’s or doctoral programs are investing additional years in education and developing specialized expertise. Repeatedly imposing such substantial fees would create an additional financial barrier to advanced education and professional development.

Requested Action

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 subsequent OPT fee under 8 CFR 214.13(i)(1)–(2), reject the alternative of repeating the $70,000 fee at higher educational levels, and consider more targeted, evidence-based approaches to preventing OPT fraud.

Protecting American workers and maintaining the integrity of immigration programs are legitimate and important objectives. However, these goals should be achieved through effective enforcement and oversight, not by imposing disproportionate financial barriers on legitimate international students, educational institutions, and employers.

Thank you for considering my comment.

I oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT participation. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and pursue targeted, proportionate measures addressing demonstrated fraud and abuse.
Preventing fraudulent employment and protecting American workers are legitimate objectives. However, imposing an extraordinary financial barrier on every participating institution and student does not distinguish legitimate educational and professional activity from misconduct. Ability to finance a $70,000 payment is not evidence of academic merit, immigration compliance, or a genuine employment relationship. Inability to finance it is not evidence of fraud.
Although schools would formally make these payments, the practical consequences could fall on students through increased charges or institutions declining to recommend otherwise eligible graduates. Employers and research programs could also lose access to qualified candidates. DHS should substantiate why these particular amounts are necessary and explain why less burdensome alternatives (such as employer verification, risk-based audits, site visits, and enforcement against identified offenders) would be insufficient.
The proposal also raises serious concerns for currently enrolled students. These students have already invested years of study and substantial resources under a framework that permits practical training related to their degrees. Introducing a potentially prohibitive financial condition after those commitments have been made would disrupt educational and professional plans. Any changes should meaningfully account for those existing commitments.

I also ask DHS to carefully distinguish the volume of supportive submissions from the substance of the arguments they contain.
Several published comments reproduce the same passage beginning, “Optional Practical Training (OPT) was created out of thin air and needs to be eliminated.” Examples include comments ICEB-2026-0100-0034 and ICEB-2026-0100-0036. Both support the proposed fees while expressing a preference for eliminating OPT altogether.
People are entitled to participate through a shared template, and doing so does not invalidate their views. However, repetition does not provide independent corroboration. An unsupported assertion does not become better supported because it appears under multiple names.
The repeated passage makes sweeping claims about OPT’s authorization, wage requirements, and protections for American workers without supplying supporting analysis. DHS should evaluate those claims against the applicable framework and evidence, rather than treating their repetition as proof. The same standard should apply to comments opposing the proposal.

There is also a substantive distinction between demonstrating that these fees would effectively address fraud and supporting them because they would discourage participation in a program the commenter wishes to abolish. The latter expresses a policy preference; it does not establish that the proposed fee amounts are necessary, proportionate, or effective.
The central question is whether DHS can justify this specific measure through reliable evidence and a reasoned assessment of its consequences. Repeated slogans cannot substitute for that justification.
I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposed fees and pursue measures that target actual misconduct while preserving meaningful access to legitimate practical training.

I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial OPT fee and $30,000 fee for subsequent OPT authorization.

One of the fundamental reasons the United States has maintained its global leadership in technology, science, and innovation is its ability to attract talented people from around the world. Many international students come to the United States for higher education and, through OPT, have the opportunity to apply their knowledge and contribute to American companies, research institutions, and the broader economy. This ability to attract and retain global talent is one of America's greatest competitive advantages.

Imposing such substantial fees would discourage many talented international students from choosing to study in the United States in the first place. The consequences would extend far beyond lost tuition revenue. More importantly, the policy would undermine the very foundation of America's long-term competitiveness: its ability to attract the world's brightest minds.

Recent enrollment trends already provide a warning. According to the Institute of International Education, new international student enrollment has already declined while graduate enrollment declined simultaneously. Domestic enrollment has not necessarily replaced these losses, particularly at the graduate level. Declining international enrollment can create financial pressure on universities, potentially leading to reduced doctoral admissions, fewer research opportunities, and cuts to faculty and university staff positions. These consequences ultimately affect American students and workers as well.

Some argue that international students take scholarships or university places away from American citizens. However, this argument overlooks important distinctions. Many federal student aid programs are restricted to U.S. citizens and eligible noncitizens, while university funding sources have their own eligibility rules. International students therefore cannot simply be assumed to be competing for the same scholarships. Furthermore, fewer international students do not automatically translate into more opportunities for domestic students, especially when universities lose revenue and reduce their academic programs.

If the goal is to build a merit-based system and expand educational opportunities for American students, discouraging talented international students through excessive OPT fees is the wrong approach. A more constructive solution would be to increase investment in universities, research funding, and educational opportunities for domestic students while preserving America's ability to attract exceptional international talent.

Protecting American workers and maintaining the integrity of the immigration system are legitimate goals. However, these objectives should be pursued through targeted oversight and enforcement rather than fees that would make practical training financially inaccessible to many qualified graduates.

Requiring universities to pay tens of thousands of dollars per OPT recommendation could result in higher tuition for all students, reduced educational services, or increased pressure on public budgets. The proposed rule would require DSOs to discriminate between their students submitting OPT requests. Nowhere do the regulations provide for prioritizing students based on financial resources, employment prospects, or other criteria to discriminate between eligible students. 

The proposed rule does not address the problem DHS is trying to solve. This failure happens in three places:
1)	There is no evidence provided that students with fewer financial resources are more likely to engage in fraud. A student or school’s financial resources has no direct relationship to compliance in external employment. Such financial barriers may actually exclude students from participating in legitimate and valuable opportunities. 
2)	More effective means of countering fraud and abuse would be to increase employer checks, site visits, and training plans, all of which have been rejected without explanation by DHS. I strongly oppose the proposed $70,000 initial and $30,000 subsequent OPT fees [1, p. 64566] and urge DHS to withdraw this rule. It would weaken the U.S. economy, punish honest students for the fraud of a few, and hand the world's best young talent to America's competitors.
 
1. It harms the U.S. economy (Section VII.A). International students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported about 355,000 jobs in the 2024-25 academic year [2]. Most of that money comes from abroad [3], and DHS itself acknowledges that schools could lose enrollment if students are deterred by the fees [1, p. 64588]. DHS's own primary estimate is $4.1 billion in costs every year, about $35 billion over ten years, yet DHS lists the rule's monetized benefits as "Not Estimated" [1, Tables 1 and 10]. A rule with tens of billions in costs and no quantified benefit should not be finalized.
 
2. It punishes honest students instead of fraudsters (Sections IV.A and IV.C). The fee is the same for every student and is not tied to any employer or fraud indicator [1, p. 64577]. DHS cites more than 10,000 students working for suspect employers [1, p. 64571]; that is a small fraction of the roughly 290,000 OPT and STEM OPT authorizations in 2024 alone [1, Table 2]. Fraud should be fought by targeting fraudulent employers and schools through site visits, E-Verify, and employer vetting. And because the fees go to the general Treasury, not to SEVP, not one dollar would fund fraud investigations [1, p. 64576].
 
3. It selects by wealth, not talent (Sections IV.C and VI). DHS admits schools may pass the fee on to students [1, p. 64575]. A STEM student could face $100,000 [1, p. 64583], or $130,000 with pre-completion OPT [1, p. 64577]. A brilliant young engineer from a modest family would be priced out, while a wealthier but less qualified student would not. That is the opposite of choosing "the most promising students" [1, p. 64574]. Small schools would be hit hardest: DHS estimates 98 small institutions would face costs above 20% of annual revenue [1, Table 15].
 
4. It gives our talent to competitors, including China. Other countries are competing hard for exactly the students this rule pushes away. In October 2025 China launched its K visa, which lets young foreign STEM graduates come and work without an employer sponsor [4]. If the United States charges $70,000 for one year of practical training, why would a top student not choose China or another competitor instead? Those graduates would then build their companies there. Today, 24% of U.S. billion-dollar startups have a founder who first came here as an international student [5]. If America wants to lead in AI, semiconductors, aerospace, and biotech, it must compete for this talent, not tax it.
 
5. It breaks faith with current students (Section VI). Many students already enrolled, including those in multi-year PhD programs, chose the United States expecting OPT to be available. Calling that expectation "speculative" [1, p. 64579] ignores real decisions about years of study and money already invested here.
 
 
American universities train these students with American resources. OPT lets that investment pay off here, through skilled work, research, and new companies, instead of sending it to our competitors. I urge DHS to withdraw this rule and fight fraud through targeted enforcement against the actual bad actors.
 
Respectfully

I am an early-career software engineer with a U.S. master's degree in computer science, on post-completion OPT at a technology company in the San Francisco Bay Area, paid at market rate. I ask DHS to withdraw this rule, or at minimum to fix the transition provision described in point 1.

1. The rule penalizes students already on OPT, and its transition text is internally inconsistent (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(2)-(3); Sec. V.C, VI).

Under 214.13(i)(2), the $30,000 fee applies only to a student who "has previously paid the initial OPT fee of $70,000." A student whose initial OPT began before the effective date never paid that fee, so the STEM extension would cost $70,000. A student who starts OPT after the effective date would pay $30,000 for the identical extension. The RIA confirms this reading: its Year 1 model assumes STEM OPT participants pay $70,000. DHS gives no reason for charging more to the students with the strongest reliance interests.

Those interests are concrete. Students on initial OPT accepted jobs, signed leases, and declined other options in reliance on the 24-month extension under the 2016 rule; employers invested in I-983 training plans. Calling these interests "outweighed" in one sentence is not the weighing required by DHS v. Regents, 591 U.S. 1 (2020).

My own STEM OPT recommendation will likely be dated after the proposed effective date. My school would owe $70,000, likely passed to me or my employer, for work I already perform lawfully. No fraud is involved.

Request: exempt from all fees any STEM extension for a student whose initial OPT EAD was approved before the effective date.

2. The fee is a revenue measure, not a condition of admission (Sec. IV.C).

DHS states that the fee is not based on processing cost, will be deposited in the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts under 31 U.S.C. 3302, will not fund ICE or SEVP, and was set to be "comparable" to H-1B fees. DHS projects $12.8 billion in annual transfers. A charge unrelated to the cost of any service and paid into the general fund is a tax. INA 214(a) authority over the "time and conditions" of admission is not taxing power (see National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974)). A federal court vacated the $100,000 H-1B payment on this ground (California v. Mullin, D. Mass. June 8, 2026).

3. The fee cannot address the fraud DHS describes (Sec. IV.A, IV.C).

DHS cites about 10,000 students tied to suspect employers. In 2024, 194,554 students were on OPT and 165,524 on STEM OPT. The fee falls on all of them. It is also paid before the DSO recommendation and, in DHS's words, "would not be tied to a specific employer." The fraud described occurs at the employer and worksite; a fee paid before an employer is known cannot screen for it, and because the money goes to the Treasury it adds no investigative capacity. Aligning the financial commitment of OPT with the costs associated with primary employment visas removes the incentive for organizations to bypass congressionally mandated H-1B limits and fee structures.
• Enhancing Institutional Accountability: By making educational institutions the primary entities responsible for filing the fee, the rule ensures that universities remain active participants in monitoring compliance, rather than treating post-graduation work authorization as an unvetted benefit.

As a concerned citizen and taxpayer I strongly support the Department of Homeland Security in publishing this notice of proposed rulemaking regarding Optional Practical Training fees. The empirical data and investigative findings cited by the Department demonstrate beyond any reasonable doubt that the current Optional Practical Training system suffers from profound systemic vulnerabilities and widespread fraudulent exploitation. Specifically, recent enforcement investigations identified more than ten thousand nonimmigrant students engaged in practical training while working for highly suspect employers across multiple states. These investigations uncovered egregious violations including empty buildings, false claims of employment, residential addresses listed as corporate headquarters with zero employees present, tax liens, suspicious offshore transactions and phantom employees who never reported for work.

Critics and potential litigants who attempt to minimize these findings ignore the massive and unsustainable administrative burden placed on federal enforcement agencies. The Student and Exchange Visitor Program manages thousands of certified institutions across numerous regional territories with a severely limited number of field representatives. Conducting complex multilayered site visits and investigating coordinated employer clusters with identical websites or shared personnel requires extraordinary time, coordination and resources. Without the proposed fee structure the Department cannot adequately resource its oversight operations or prevent bad actors from exploiting practical training as an informal and unlimited employment benefit.

Furthermore, historical enforcement actions validate the immediate necessity of this rule. Federal authorities previously convicted individuals who operated shell companies providing false employment verification documents and fake offer letters to thousands of foreign students in exchange for illegal fees. These criminal enterprises directly facilitated visa fraud and compromised national security. The proposed fees of seventy thousand dollars for initial authorization and thirty thousand dollars for subsequent extensions create a vital and rational financial deterrent. This fee structure ensures that participating institutions exercise proper oversight and selectivity rather than rubber-stamping applications for profit.

Beyond the immediate implementation of these robust fees, the Department must recognize that incremental financial barriers remain an incomplete remedy for a fundamentally flawed program. The systemic displacement of American workers, the ongoing evasion of statutory H-1B visa caps and the persistent structural incentives for cheap foreign labor demonstrate that the Optional Practical Training program should be canceled altogether. Practical training was originally conceived as a limited and supervised educational adjunct rather than an open-ended corporate labor pipeline. In the context of judicial review under the Administrative Procedure Act, the Department has established an unimpeachable rational connection between the empirical evidence of fraud and the chosen regulatory remedy. The Secretary of Homeland Security possesses broad and unambiguous statutory authority under section 214 of the Immigration and Nationality Act and the Homeland Security Act of 2002 to administer immigration laws and prescribe the time and conditions of alien admission. Establishing conditions that combat fraud, protect domestic labor markets and ensure economic security falls squarely within the primary mission of the Department. Any legal challenge brought against this rule or subsequent actions toward program cancellation would fail to recognize that the agency has acted reasonably and proportionately to safeguard the integrity of the immigration system against pervasive abuse. To the Department of Homeland Security:

I strongly support the proposed rule establishing fees of $70,000 for initial Optional Practical Training (OPT) and $30,000 for subsequent OPT authorizations. However, I believe these amounts are too low and encourage DHS to consider significantly higher fees.

My position is straightforward: American immigration policy should serve American citizens, not provide corporations and universities with an inexpensive pipeline into the domestic labor market.

1. If these are truly the world’s best and brightest, the fees should reflect that.

We repeatedly hear that foreign workers and international graduates possess extraordinary skills that American employers supposedly cannot find domestically.

If these individuals are genuinely the next Einsteins, groundbreaking innovators, and irreplaceable scientific minds, why should a $70,000 or even substantially higher fee be considered unreasonable?

Truly exceptional talent should be capable of demonstrating extraordinary economic or scientific value. Institutions and employers claiming that such talent is indispensable should be prepared to substantiate those claims.

The United States has no obligation to subsidize corporate access to international labor simply because employers prefer a larger applicant pool.

2. OPT should not function as an alternative employment visa program.

F-1 status exists primarily for education. OPT has expanded opportunities for foreign students to participate in the American labor market beyond their academic studies.

DHS itself identifies concerns involving fraud, program integrity, and the potential use of OPT to circumvent H-1B fees and requirements.

These concerns deserve meaningful regulatory action.

The United States should not allow temporary educational status to become an inexpensive substitute for employment-based immigration procedures.

3. American graduates deserve priority.

American students invest considerable time and financial resources in obtaining degrees, particularly in engineering, computer science, technology, and other technical disciplines.

Their employment prospects should matter when federal agencies evaluate programs that increase the supply of available labor.

Employers claiming domestic talent shortages should demonstrate that they have offered competitive compensation, invested in training, and made meaningful efforts to recruit qualified Americans.

Expanding access to foreign labor should not become a substitute for developing the domestic workforce.

4. Corporate inconvenience is not sufficient justification for low fees.

Universities and employers may argue that these costs discourage international recruitment or limit participation.

That is not necessarily a defect in the policy.

If the objective is to discourage routine reliance on OPT while preserving access where institutions can justify the substantial expense, the fee should be high enough to influence institutional decisions.

DHS should evaluate higher initial and subsequent fees, with a transparent economic and legal justification.

Importantly, the proposed rule places payment responsibility on educational institutions. DHS should also examine whether schools might transfer these costs to students or receive indirect reimbursement from employers, and establish appropriate disclosure and enforcement safeguards.

5. Protecting the domestic labor market is a legitimate national objective.

The economic interests of universities, multinational corporations, and immigration beneficiaries are not automatically identical to those of American workers.

The relevant questions are whether OPT delivers measurable benefits to the United States, whether program participants fill genuinely unmet needs, and whether the program affects domestic hiring, wages, and career opportunities.

Those questions should be evaluated using evidence rather than assertions that foreign labor is inherently indispensable.

Conclusion

I support finalizing the proposed OPT fee rule, but recommend increasing the proposed $70,000 initial fee and $30,000 subsequent fee.

If institutions and employers truly believe these candidates possess rare, extraordinary, and economically indispensable abilities, they should be able to demonstrate that value.

If substantially higher fees make routine OPT recruitment uneconomical, that outcome should prompt serious examination of whether the program was being used for exceptional talent or simply convenient access to additional labor.

American workers should not be expected to compete against an international labor pipeline structured around the convenience of employers and educational institutions.
